newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN/OAU plan crisis talks on African refugees.
newsitem.headline: UN/OAU plan crisis talks on African refugees.

text.p: The United Nations and Organisation of African Unity (OAU) plan to hold talks early next month on how to better protect some 500,000 Rwandan and Burundi refugees, a UNHCR spokeswoman said on Friday.

Spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole also said the U.N. refugee agency continued to receive disturbing reports that Rwandan Hutu refugees are being "persecuted or even killed by soldiers" in some areas of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) -- which denounced Gabon this week for expelling its last 168 Rwandans -- is worried about mounting pressure throughout host countries in Africa's Great Lakes region to deport Burundians and Rwandans.

The Geneva-based agency, relying on field reports from its staff and U.N. human rights monitors, believes it is not safe for many Burundians and Rwandans to go home because of violence between Tutsi-led armies and armed Hutus in their homelands.
However, it helps repatriate those refugees who choose to go and those who face more danger in their country of asylum.
Sadako Ogata, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, has discussed the coming talks with OAU secretary general Salim Salim and U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan, according to the spokeswoman.

"The High Commissioner is deeply concerned that the situation for refugees in the Great Lakes is steadily worsening, with basic principles of asylum becoming increasingly difficult to uphold," O'Toole told a news briefing in Geneva.
"She has been taking urgent action to try to address what she describes as a 'crisis of protection' in Africa," she added.
No exact date or exact venue has been set for the talks, to be convened in Africa by the OAU, but it was hoped they could be held before the U.N. General Assembly opens in mid-September.

Abuses continue in ex-Zaire -- where 200,000 Rwandans remain unaccounted for since reported massacres during a seven-month-long campaign by forces of rebel leader Laurent Kabila that toppled veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May.
The Kabila rebels were dominated by ethnic Tutsis and backed by Rwandan Tutsi soldiers, many of whom are still in the renamed Democratic Republic of the Congo.

"Although the authorities in some areas are being cooperative, in others we still hear reports of soldiers being involved in driving refugees deeper into the jungle or even killing them," O'Toole said of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

"The government of the DRC alleges that the refugees -- some of whom are ex-Far or Interahamwe -- are involved in fighting in some parts of the country," she added. "They want to repatriate them as soon as possible."
The UNHCR is negotiating with Kinshasa authorities to start screening refugees who do not want to return, O'Toole said.

Both Angola and the Central African Republic, which are screening several thousand Rwandans to determine whether they deserve asylum, "have made it clear they want these people to leave as soon as possible", according to O'Toole.
In Tanzania, home to 30,000 Rwandans, UNHCR has received reports that the "authorities are rounding these people up and forcibly sending them back". It also has 300,000 Burundians.
"Given all these pressures, the High Commissioner believes that some sort of strategy has to be worked out to ensure that those who need protection receive it," O'Toole said.

"While there may be people among the remaining refugees who have been involved in some way in the Rwandan genocide, there are also innocent men, women and children who desperately need and deserve our help and international protection," she added.
